list.listitem: Tendinopathy is a diagnosis based on a constellation of clinical findings. There is no single physical examination test that is pathognomonic for any of the different tendinopathies. C
Acute conservative treatment includes rest C and ice. B
Limited evidence suggests that analgesics (acetaminophen) and NSAIDs provide pain relief; the data on corticosteroid injections are mixed. B
Exercise therapy with a focus on eccentric strengthening is the most effective treatment for many forms of tendinopathy. B

background.definition: Tendinopathy is a chronic, degenerative, noninflammatory condition affecting the collagen bundles of the muscle tendon. Tendinopathy produces localized activity-related pain of insidious onset. Tendinopathy is a generalized term made through clinical diagnosis. Tendinosis refers to the histologic change in the tendon seen with most tendinopathies. Tendinitis refers to acute inflammatory change to the tendon, which may be self-limited, or may progress to a noninflammatory tendinopathy of subacute or chronic duration.

list.listitem: Rotator cuff tendinopathy: 1% to 2% of the general population; 20% to 30% incidence in throwing sports
Lateral epicondylitis: 1% to 2% of the general population; up to 40% incidence in racquet sports
Patellar tendinopathy: less than 1% of the general population; 14% to 20% in athletes
Achilles tendinopathy: 1% to 2% of the general population; 7% to 11% of runners

Rotator cuff tendinopathy: throwing sports, hand-over-head activities. A systematic review of 16 studies concluded that age over 50 years (OR 3.3), diabetes (OR 2.2), and work with the shoulder above 90 degrees (OR 2.4) increased the likelihood of rotator cuff tendinopathy.
Lateral and medial epicondylitis: racquet sports (lateral), golf (medial), wrist extension/supination against resistance (lateral)
Patellar tendinopathy: jumping, other sports with explosive quadriceps use (volleyball, soccer, distance running)
Achilles tendinopathy: poor flexibility, malalignment, rapid increase in physical training schedule, distance running, soccer, football, volleyball, basketball

A widely cited model is the "continuum" model of tendon pathology, which describes tendinopathy as a continuum with three stages: reactive tendinopathy, tendon disrepair, and degenerative tendinopathy.

Reactive tendinopathy: the initial injury (overload from excessive tensile or compressive forces) results in a non-inflammatory proliferative response in the cells and matrix of the tendon, resulting in thickening of the effected portion of the tendon (this is different from normal adaption which is an increase in stiffness of the tendon).

Tendon disrepair: attempted repair with an increase of cells which produce protein (collagen and proteoglycan), which leads to matrix separation and disorganization (matrix breakdown is what differentiates this from reactive tendinopathy). This weakens the tendon.

Degenerative tendinopathy: progression of cellular and matrix changes leads to areas of apoptosis, resulting in areas of acellularity, little collagen, and breakdown products. Stress placed on the tendon during this stage can result in rupture of the tendon.

Injuries can be reduced by incorporating exercises specifically aimed at improving proprioception, strength, and balance. A 30-minute exercise program, performed 2 to 3 times per week, reduced the number of noncontact leg injuries by 66%.
Balance training is effective in preventing Achilles and patellar tendinopathy, but data is limited.
Data is mixed regarding lower extremity orthoses to prevent Achilles tendinopathy.
Tendinopathy is a diagnosis based on a constellation of clinical features; no single examination finding is pathognomonic. C
Typical features include pain with repetitive activity, localized tenderness with palpation, and/or pain when testing muscular resistance parallel to the path of the injured tendon. C

Imaging is not required for diagnosis; if used, MRI may show an abnormal signal within the tendon and tendon thickening. Ultrasound is increasingly used to evaluate tendons. On ultrasound, the tendinopathic tendon appears thickened with a heterogeneous or "speckled" and disorganized appearance. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Radiographic evidence, focal osseous tenderness to palpation
Visible, palpable, or radiographic evidence for tendon defect
Radicular pain distribution, no increase with resisted joint motion

list.listitem: Patients with tendinopathy describe the insidious onset of dull pain with exercise. Over time the pain becomes more severe with activity and may persist at rest.
Patients may or may not report a period of overuse or overtraining that precedes the pain.
Examination reveals pain that is exacerbated by resisted motion and specific examination tests of the tendon.
If anatomically possible, direct palpation of the problematic tendon will result in reproducible pain.
See chapters on specific diagnoses for additional detail on the clinical examination: medial and lateral epicondylitis, achilles tendinitis, and rotator cuff tendinitis.
MRI or ultrasound can be used if diagnosis is in doubt (especially when the tendon is not anatomically accessible for palpation).
MRI is best for global assessment of joint/tendon region, while ultrasound is best for dynamic imaging (simultaneous imaging and examining).
Imaging can be useful to distinguish a tendon rupture (complete or partial) from tendinopathy.
See chapters on specific diagnoses for additional detail on the clinical examination: medial and lateral epicondylitis, achilles tendinitis, and rotator cuff tendinitis.

Patients typically present with localized pain of insidious onset aggravated by specific repetitive activity or motion. They may have point tenderness with palpation and pain provoked with resistance parallel to the path of the tendon and/or with specialized tests.
Consider imaging (ultrasound, MRI) if the diagnosis is in question.

Begin treatment with protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation (PRICE) and analgesics or NSAIDs. Consider steroid injections for short-term pain relief and physical therapy with eccentric strengthening for chronic tendinopathy.
Initial conservative therapy for tendinopathy includes relative rest C and ice. B
Analgesics are a common adjunct for initial therapy, although evidence for their efficacy is limited. B
Physical therapy with focus on eccentric strengthening exercises shows promise for both pain control and faster recovery in chronic tendinosis. B
Topical nitroglycerin can be effective in the short term to intermediate term (<6 months of symptoms).B
Current evidence shows weak or uncertain benefit for corticosteroid injections, platelet rich plasma injections, bracing, iontophoresis, phonophoresis, and extracorporeal shock wave therapy. B
There is no consistent evidence that NSAIDs are superior to acetaminophen for short-term pain relief (which is consistent with the theory that tendinopathy is largely noninflammatory in nature).

Both NSAIDs and acetaminophen can be used. There is only moderate evidence in systematic reviews for either medication's effectiveness in pain control and no evidence that either NSAIDs or acetaminophen alter or improve disease course.

Topical nitroglycerin is superior to placebo (with the exception of patellar tendinopathy) in the short term to intermediate term (<6 months of symptoms), though more data for long term outcomes is needed.

Corticosteroid peritendinous injections may provide short-term pain relief in many forms of tendinopathy, but evidence is inconsistent, and there is a risk of tendon weakening and rupture following this injection.

Surgical consultation may be considered if tendinopathy is failing to respond to treatment after 3 to 6 months of conservative therapy. However, the quality of evidence to support its efficacy is largely poor.
Corticosteroid injections of the elbow and shoulder may provide short term benefit compared to placebo, but has not been shown to be superior to NSAIDs.
There is insufficient evidence to support the use of platelet rich therapies for musculoskeletal soft tissue injuries.
Platelet-rich plasma injection has mixed data for patellar tendinopathy; no benefit from one injection, but some studies suggest that multiple injections are effective.

A Cochrane review identified only two studies with a total of 92 patients comparing surgery with exercise in one study and sclerosing injections in the other. Surgery did not to provide any meaningful benefit.
Platelet-rich plasma injection has some data to support use in lateral epicondylitis. Data is mixed regarding benefit of leukocyte rich versus poor.
Corticosteroid injections are effective for trigger finger.
Prolotherapy and sclerotherapy has some data to support use for Achilles tendinopathy.
Platelet-rich plasma injection is no more effective than saline for Achilles tendinopathy.
Peritendinous autologous blood injections added to calf strengthening exercises are not beneficial in Achilles tendinopathy.
Ultrasound guided steroid injections may offer some additional benefit over physical therapy alone.
Exercise therapy, especially eccentric exercise therapy, is assuming an increasingly universal role in treatment of chronic tendinosis.

Eccentric exercises are activities in which muscles and tendons are elongating while the muscle is contracting. For example, a slow single-leg squat from standing position to a knee flexed position results in eccentric quadriceps contraction.
Exercise therapy results in a high rate of pain relief and even cure for most common forms of tendinosis.
There is limited data to support counterforce bracing for lateral epicondylitis.
Extracorporeal shock wave therapy has limited data supporting its use in rotator cuff and patellar tendinopathy.
Iontophoresis and phonophoresis are common physical therapy modalities and bracing techniques. Each is of uncertain benefit in tendinopathy.
Low intensity pulsed ultrasound is not beneficial in chronic patellar tendinopathy.
Radial extracorporeal shock-wave therapy is not beneficial in chronic rotator cuff tendinitis.
High-energy extracorporeal shock-wave therapy may be beneficial for chronic calcific tendinitis of the shoulder.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend deep transverse friction massage for lateral elbow or lateral knee tendinitis.
There is no evidence supporting biopsychosocial rehabilitation for work-related tendinopathy.
Most patients with tendinopathy (>80%) will recover within 3 to 6 months with appropriate conservative management, including exercise therapy. B

A minority of patients may require surgical consultation. However, given the high rate of recovery, conservative treatment for tendinopathy should be used for at least 6 months before proceeding to surgical consultation. C
Lack of appropriate therapy, inadequate rest from offending activities, and poor biomechanics may predispose a person to chronic persistence of symptoms. C
